newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba restricts internal migration to Havana.
newsitem.headline: Cuba restricts internal migration to Havana.

text.p: Cuba, moving to reduce overcrowding, unemployment and delinquency in Havana, imposed restrictions on Saturday on the migration of residents from the island's rural areas to the capital.

A government decree published in the official Communist Party newspaper Granma required citizens living outside the capital who wanted to move permanently to Havana to obtain prior authorization from local city authorities.

Migration to the capital without the necessary authorization would be punishable by varying fines of between 200 and 1,000 Cuban pesos (around US$10 to US$50). Offenders would also be sent back to their places of origin.

A non-Havana resident must request permission to live in a house in the capital. Then officials in the area where he or she planned to live would decide whether the house had the space and conditions to take the new arrivals.
The curbs followed a public call from President Fidel Castro this month for a crackdown on "social indiscipline" in Havana, where more than two million of the island's 11 million population live.

Castro said in an April 4 speech that uncontrolled migration to Havana, especially from the east of the communist-ruled island, had resulted in overcrowding, the creation of shantytowns, unemployment and increased crime.
It had also put tremendous strain on Havana's deteriorated public utilities and transportation system.
The restrictions applied particularly to the municipalities of Habana Vieja, Centro Habana, Cerro and Diez de Octubre, where problems of overcrowding were especially acute.

Foreign diplomats in Havana said they expected authorities would also use the new regulations to crack down on forms of delinquency like prostitution. Those from outside Havana caught operating illegally in the capital could now be swiftly sent home to their provinces.
